1786 · Ecueracapa, speaking for the western Comanche, met Governor Juan Bautista de Anza here and ended a generation of war with New Mexico.
1835 · Near the Canadian River. The first treaty between the United States and the Comanche, signed after the dragoon expedition Catlin rode with.
1844 · Near present-day Waco. Sam Houston's Republic of Texas made peace with the Penateka, four years after the Council House killings.
1846 · Near the Brazos River. Signed months after Texas joined the United States, it put the southern Comanche under U.S. 'protection' but drew no boundary at all.
1847 · On the Pedernales River. Penateka chiefs and John O. Meusebach of the German colonists made a private peace, widely described as never broken.
1850 · Near the San Saba River in Texas. A frontier line the Senate never ratified.
1851 · A council on the San Saba River. It bound the southern Comanche to stop raids into Mexico, and was never ratified.
1853 · South of the Arkansas River in present-day Kansas, on the Santa Fe Trail.
1865 · A council ground near present-day Wichita, Kansas.
1867 · Seventy miles south of Fort Larned. The treaty that created the Kiowa-Comanche-Apache reservation and promised hunting rights south of the Arkansas.
1892 · Negotiated at Fort Sill. It broke up the reservation into allotments and opened the rest to settlers.
1680–1706 · After the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Spanish horses spread onto the plains. In 1706 Spanish officials here wrote the first known record of the name Comanche.
March 19, 1840 · Penateka leaders came to make peace and were killed when Texans tried to take them prisoner.
August 1840 · Buffalo Hump's warriors rode all the way to the Gulf and burned this port town.
August 12, 1840 · Near present-day Lockhart. Texans caught the returning raiders in a running fight.
June 27, 1874 · Comanche, Cheyenne, Kiowa, and Arapaho warriors led by Quanah and Isatai attacked the hide hunters' post. The attack failed.
September 28, 1874 · The Army attacked the canyon camps at dawn, burned the winter food, and killed the horse herd at Tule Canyon.
1875 · In late May and early June 1875 Quanah led the Quahadi in. The free life on the southern plains was over.
June 1834 · The First Dragoons set out from here, with George Catlin riding along to paint.
July 1834 · Catlin painted the Comanche camp in a valley with granite mountains beyond, east of the Wichita Mountains. Its exact spot isn't known.
July 21–22, 1834 · The dragoons marched west through the Wichita Mountains to council here with Wichita, Comanche, and Kiowa leaders.
December 1860 · Texas Rangers attacked the camp of Quanah's family and carried off his mother, Nautda (Cynthia Ann Parker), and his sister.
c. 1890 · today near Cache · Quanah's two-story home with ten stars on the roof. It has been moved twice and now stands on private land near Cache. Not open to visitors.
1957 · In Fort Sill's post cemetery, where Quanah was reburied beside his mother and sister.
1871–1980 · A boarding school for Native children for 109 years. The 1904 stone girls' dormitory still stands.
Open Mon–Sat · Free · 701 NW Ferris Ave, Lawton. The Comanche Nation's own museum, with galleries on Comanche history, the code talkers, and Comanche artists.

Story 1How a mountain people became the greatest horse riders on the plains.

Before 1700 The Comanche were once part of the Shoshone, living in the high country to the north and west. Around 1700 their language began to separate from Shoshone, and they began moving south and east onto the plains.

1680 In 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico rose up and drove the Spanish out of their country for more than a decade. Spanish horses scattered. Through trade and raiding, they spread north and east among the peoples of the plains.
